solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Disorderly, hungover husband leaves nick with half-cut male

indicators.note: to leave is to depart, so the husband (H) walks out of HUNGOVER and the letters close up behind him
cut in half, MALE keeps only one of its two halves, here the back end

parts.note: to nick is to nab, i.e. arrest

explanation.surface: A drunk husband staggers out of the police station with an equally tipsy man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for drunk, which suits the hungover husband, but here it simply trims MALE to its last two letters. 'Nick' is British slang for a police station, but it works as the verb 'arrest'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone ungovernable cannot be kept in order, which is what disorderly describes.

clue.text: Tremulous at heart, groom left after meal

indicators.note: the heart of anything is its centre, so only the central letter of the word is wanted

parts.note: the middle (fifth) letter of the nine-letter TREMULOUS
to groom is to tidy, neaten

explanation.surface: A nervous bridegroom is abandoned once the wedding breakfast is over.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'groom' a bridegroom and 'left' his jilting; in fact 'groom' is the verb to tidy and 'left after meal' is the whole definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive phrase for the adjective: food nobody ate is what remains on the plate once the meal is over.

clue.text: Chap concealing new note about revolutionary weapons

indicators.note: a revolution is a turning round, so the word it touches, RE, is turned back to front
to conceal is to hide inside

parts.note: a guy is a chap; he goes round the rest
n. is the abbreviation for note

explanation.surface: A man hides guns for a revolutionary cause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like a noun for a rebel hiding arms; it is an adjective applied to 'about'. N for note is the dictionary abbreviation, not a musical note.
explanation.definitionFit: A collective sense: gunnery can mean heavy guns taken together, a force's weapons.

clue.text: Second-hand vehicle covered by six promissory notes

indicators.note: something covered has other things over it on both sides

parts.note: IOUs are written promises to pay

explanation.surface: Someone pays for a used car with a handful of IOUs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second-hand vehicle' reads as a used car, but the hyphenated word is the definition on its own, in the sense of experienced through others.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: vicarious experience comes through someone else, so it is second-hand rather than lived directly.

clue.text: Cadre beaten up and shot

indicators.note: something beaten up is knocked out of shape, so the letters of CADRE are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Members of a party cadre are assaulted and then shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' looks like gunfire in a violent surface; it is the verb of speed, as in 'shot past'.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb of speed: a car that shot past went very fast, so it raced.

clue.text: Settle on Scottish island, coming home at last

parts.note: Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde

indicators.note: at last means finally, so each of the two words before gives only its final letter

parts.note: last letters of comING and homE

explanation.surface: Someone decides to settle on a Scottish island, finally coming home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settle on' reads as making a home somewhere; 'Settle' alone is the definition, in the sense of fixing details, and 'on' puts ARRAN above the rest in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of fixing details: to settle a date or a deal is to arrange it.

clue.text: Starts to learn all about colour of milk

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so each of the next three words gives its opening letter

parts.note: first letters of Learn, All, About

explanation.surface: A pupil begins learning about what colour milk really is.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an adjectival phrase: lacteal means of or relating to milk, which is why 'of milk' swaps in for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A technical adjective from Latin lac, milk: lacteal describes anything relating to milk.

clue.text: I for one desperately mourn real man

indicators.note: acting desperately means acting wildly, so the letters are thrown into a frantic new order

explanation.surface: Someone speaking for themselves admits to grieving hard for a genuine man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I for one' reads as a speaker volunteering an opinion; it is the letter I, which stands for one.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the letter I, standing for the number one, is one instance of the Roman system.

clue.text: Vast abuse of cocaine

indicators.note: to abuse something is to misuse it and knock it about, so the letters of COCAINE are mistreated into a new order

explanation.surface: A news report on huge-scale cocaine misuse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abuse' belongs to drug talk in the surface; its job is to jumble the seven letters of COCAINE.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: oceanic means on the scale of an ocean, hence immense.

clue.text: Onset of breathlessness after clown inhales Senior Service and pipe

indicators.note: to inhale is to draw something inside yourself
the onset is the very beginning, so only the first letter is wanted

parts.note: Coco the Clown, a famous circus clown; RN goes inside him
the Royal Navy, nicknamed the Senior Service as the oldest British armed force

explanation.surface: A clown, puffing on a sailor's brand of cigarette and a pipe, starts to wheeze.
explanation.walkthrough: Senior Service was also a British cigarette brand, which is why 'inhales' fits so well; in the wordplay it is the Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: A kind of pipe named for its material: a corncob pipe has its bowl carved from a dried corn cob.

clue.text: Spooner's take on his characteristic hobby

indicators.note: Rev William Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so his version of a phrase swaps its initial sounds

parts.note: Spooner's trademark was word-botching; WORD takes the B of BOTCHING, and 'burd' is spelt BIRD
BOTCHING takes the W of WORD, and 'wotching' is spelt WATCHING

explanation.surface: A remark on the favourite pastime of the famously muddled Reverend Spooner.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is never written out: Spooner's characteristic habit was word-botching, and swapping its initial sounds gives bird-watching.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: watching wild birds is a pastime many people take up, one hobby among many.

clue.text: Insectivorous African gannets regularly breed

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so every second letter is taken

parts.note: the even letters of gANnEtS: A, N, T
to bear young is to breed

explanation.surface: A note on African seabirds that breed regularly, perhaps eating insects.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an adjective phrase standing for an animal: the antbear, or aardvark, is an African insect-eater.
explanation.definitionFit: A description standing for the animal: the antbear, another name for the aardvark, is an African mammal that feeds on ants and termites.

clue.text: Nursed a mercurial ballerina's partner

indicators.note: mercurial means volatile and changeable, so the letters shift into a new order

explanation.surface: A temperamental ballerina's partner has been nursed through an injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mercurial' suggests a moody person, the partner perhaps; it signals that NURSED A is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A description by role: a danseur is a male ballet dancer, the one who partners and lifts the ballerina.

clue.text: Charlie is popular name in New York

indicators.note: in means inside, so the letters before it are placed within New York's abbreviation

parts.note: the usual abbreviation; it goes round the rest

explanation.surface: Charlie is the fashionable baby name in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' looks like a name, but in British slang a charlie is a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A British slang sense: calling someone a proper charlie means they are a fool, a silly person.

clue.text: Fraternity member felt endlessly glum after rum

indicators.note: without its end, so FELT loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A club member drinks rum and feels miserable without end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' is the drink in the surface but the old British adjective for odd in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A specific example: the Oddfellows are a British friendly society, a fraternal order, and each member is an Oddfellow.

clue.text: Dirty dancing with dirty look

parts.note: disco is a style of dancing
to lour is to frown, a dirty look

explanation.surface: Suggestive dancing earns someone a disapproving glare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dirty dancing' reads as the film; 'Dirty' alone is the definition, used as a verb, and the second 'dirty' belongs to 'dirty look'.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb sense: to dirty a surface is to stain it, changing its colour for the worse.

clue.text: Profits from one's times abroad

indicators.note: abroad once meant widely scattered, so the letters are spread about

explanation.surface: Someone makes money from their years spent overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' completes a travel picture, but here it means widely scattered.
explanation.definitionFit: A business sense: to monetise an asset is to turn it into a source of income, so to profit from it.

clue.text: Not very musical group fronting Oscars

indicators.note: to front something is to stand before it

parts.note: O is Oscar in the NATO alphabet, so two of them

explanation.surface: A band playing at the Oscars is not very musical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oscars' suggests the film awards; it is the phonetic-alphabet word for O, doubled.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'none too pleased' means not very pleased, the phrase working as a mild negative.

clue.text: Extra digit inhibiting Pole

indicators.note: to inhibit is to hold something in check

parts.note: a toe is a digit of the foot
a spar is a pole, as on a ship

explanation.surface: A Polish person has an extra finger that holds them back.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P dresses 'Pole' as a nationality; it is a wooden pole.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: money or time to spare is more than needed, so extra.

clue.text: Beer is forbidden on street

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece sitting on another follows it

explanation.surface: Drinking beer in the street is banned.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a local bylaw against street drinking, with 'is' as a plain link.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: stout is a dark, strong type of beer, such as Guinness.

clue.text: Prepare champion for disappointment

parts.note: to set (a table, a trap) is to prepare it
to champion a cause is to back it

explanation.surface: Advice to get a champion ready for defeat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Champion' looks like a noun, the winner; it is the verb 'support'.
explanation.definitionFit: A near-synonym: a setback is a reverse in fortunes, the kind of event that disappoints.

clue.text: Celebrity chef hosting current English actor

indicators.note: a host has guests inside the house

parts.note: Jamie Oliver, the British TV chef
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A famous chef has a present-day English actor on his show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like 'present-day', describing the actor; in physics I is the symbol for current.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Laurence Olivier, famed for Shakespeare on stage and screen, is the classic English actor.

clue.text: Calls in during supper

indicators.note: in means contained within, so the answer lies inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Someone phones in the middle of dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calls in' reads as a phrasal verb, a visit; 'in' actually belongs to the wordplay, and 'during' is part of the text the answer is hidden in.
explanation.definitionFit: A British idiom: to ring someone up is to telephone them, to call them.

clue.text: Quiet sound of sheep (not black) in fold

indicators.note: 'not black' means without black, so B (black, as on pencil grades) is taken away

explanation.surface: A white sheep bleats softly in its pen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fold' is a sheep pen in the surface, which is why 'in fold' reads naturally; the definition is fold as a crease.
explanation.definitionFit: A specific kind: a pleat is a fold pressed or stitched into fabric.

clue.text: Duck — extremely succulent and fatty bird

parts.note: a duck is a score of nought in cricket, O

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its first and last letters are taken

parts.note: the first and last letters of SucculenT

explanation.surface: A menu note on duck: juicy, rich, a fatty bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' wants to be the bird of the definition; it is O, a cricketer's score of nought, and the definition is the plain 'bird' at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the ostrich, the largest flightless African runner, is one kind of bird.

clue.text: Old salt shed light on hostility

parts.note: to have shed light is to have lit

explanation.surface: An old sailor has illuminated the hostility aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old salt' is a veteran sailor in the surface; the definition means a chemical salt with an old-fashioned name.
explanation.definitionFit: An obsolete chemical name: lithate is the former term for a urate, a salt of uric acid once called lithic acid.

clue.text: Hand eggs one cracks to Head of Nutrition

indicators.note: to crack something is to break into it, so I forces its way inside TO

parts.note: used as it stands; I goes inside

indicators.note: the head is the top, so only the first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A nutrition chief is handed eggs, and someone breaks one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hand' reads as the verb to pass; it is a noun, as in 'give them a big hand'.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: giving someone a big hand means applauding, and an ovation is enthusiastic applause.

clue.text: Initially handed one shilling, penurious dons translated The Go-Between

indicators.note: to don is to put on clothing
initially means at the start, so only the first letter of handed is taken

parts.note: s. was the abbreviation for the old British shilling coin
tr. = translated; it wraps round BROKE

explanation.surface: Poor university dons, paid a shilling each, translate L. P. Hartley's novel The Go-Between.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Go-Between' is L. P. Hartley's novel, and 'dons' look like academics; here the definition is a go-between, and 'dons' means puts on. The shilling was a pre-decimal British coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A diplomatic idiom: an honest broker is a neutral party who mediates between two sides, exactly the role of a go-between.
